native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: Over 1975-2015, Sub-Saharan Africa persistently devoted a larger share of GNI to education than developing countries (LMC) - mean 4.30% vs 3.50% of GNI, converging to near parity by 2015 (3.15% vs 3.06%) - yet SSA's GNI per capita remained lower and grew more slowly in the only fully observed income window (2011-2015 CAGR 1.25% vs 3.29%). In this aggregate panel, education expenditure (% of GNI) shows no positive association with per-capita income in either group in raw levels, and the association is weaker (less negative, turning mildly positive) in Sub-Saharan Africa than in LMC once the common time trend is removed (SSA slope +0.033 vs LMC -0.200 log-points per pp of GNI; interaction delta=-0.23, HAC se 0.05). Hypothesis: the marginal payoff to education-expenditure shares is smaller in Sub-Saharan Africa than in developing countries - SSA's higher and earlier investment share did not translate into a detectable income advantage. Because SSA income is observed in only 5 of 41 years and all series are group aggregates, this comparison is suggestive and descriptive, not causal or precisely identified.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Inspected and reshaped the wide 12x45 WDI file (2 groups x 6 series, 1975-2015) to a long group-year panel (artifacts/long_panel.csv). 2) Pooled two-group OLS with HAC(1) SEs: ln(GNI) ~ edu + LMC + edu:LMC, on all 46 available income observations and on the strict 2011-2015 overlap (n=10), reporting group-specific slopes (SSA beta, LMC beta+delta) and the interaction delta with delta-method SEs. 3) Within-group diagnostics: SSA-only OLS 2011-2015 (n=5); LMC-only 1975-2015 (n=41) with and without a linear year trend; pooled model with year trend as robustness. 4) Descriptive 1975-2015 comparison of expenditure shares, enrollment ratios, correlations, and 2011-2015 income growth. 5) No imputation; complete-case throughout; documentation mismatches (GDP 2010 US$ vs GNI 2015 US$; % of total expenditure vs % of GNI; SSF vs SSA code) flagged and resolved in favor of the data.
